language.name: German
features: In statements, the finite verb normally occupies the second position.
Yes/no questions normally start with the finite verb.
A modal moves the main verb to the end in its infinitive form.
Noun negation uses forms of kein; verb negation commonly uses nicht.
Learn a noun together with its gender and the cases a verb requires.

lessons.title: First words
lessons.goal: Start and end a simple interaction
lessons.introduction: A few social expressions are conventional, not assembled by grammar. Learn these short forms as complete units.

notes.explanation: Learn these as complete expressions. You do not need to understand endings before using them.
notes.detail: Use Sie with strangers, staff, and people you do not know well. The guide uses formal address so its requests work in ordinary public situations.
notes.caution: “Bitte” is versatile: it can mean please, here you go, or a response to thanks. Context decides.

lessons.title: Needs and possession
lessons.goal: Say what you need or already have
lessons.introduction: A verb plus an interchangeable noun phrase gives you a whole family of useful statements.

notes.recipe: Ich brauche + noun phrase. / Ich habe + noun phrase.
notes.explanation: For “I need” use ich brauche. For “I have” use ich habe. The verb stays in the second position in simple statements.
notes.detail: Learn ein Ticket, einen Kaffee, Wasser, and Hilfe as ready-to-use units. German articles change with the role of a noun in the sentence.
notes.caution: Do not attach ein to every noun: Wasser and Hilfe normally have no indefinite article in these examples.

lessons.title: What you would like
lessons.introduction: One courteous construction works with many objects. Substitute the thing you want instead of memorizing an order.

notes.explanation: Ich möchte is a courteous way to say what you would like. It works well in shops, cafés, and at counters.
notes.detail: The article is part of the noun phrase: einen Kaffee, ein Ticket, but simply Wasser. For a question to the listener, the verb comes first: Möchten Sie …?
notes.caution: Ich will expresses “I want” more directly and can sound demanding as an order. Prefer ich möchte when asking for a product.

lessons.title: Yes/no questions
lessons.introduction: A question changes the form of a whole clause. The same mechanism works with several verbs.

notes.explanation: For yes/no questions, put the conjugated verb first: Haben Sie …? Sprechen Sie …? The statement equivalent starts with the subject.
notes.detail: Sie is the formal “you.” Its verb forms usually match the infinitive: haben, sprechen, verstehen.
notes.caution: A question does not need a separate “do” helper in German.

lessons.title: Ask for help
lessons.introduction: A question, a modal verb and an action can be combined. Change the recipient or action to make a new request.

notes.explanation: Können Sie is a productive and courteous question starter. The action verb stays in its infinitive form at the end.
notes.detail: Helfen requires a dative recipient: mir for “me,” Ihnen for formal “you.” This is why “help me” is mir helfen.
notes.caution: Bitte is optional, but useful. Keep the infinitive at the end: Können Sie mir helfen?

lessons.title: When you do not understand
lessons.introduction: Say what you cannot understand and ask for clarification instead of trying to guess.

notes.recipe: Ich verstehe das nicht. / Sprechen Sie bitte langsam.
notes.explanation: Nicht is the common negative word for a verb phrase. Say plainly when you do not understand rather than guessing.
notes.detail: The short request Sprechen Sie bitte langsam is a conventional polite imperative. Memorize it whole for now.
notes.caution: German has two major negation strategies: nicht and kein. The negation lesson compares them.

lessons.title: Places and directions
lessons.goal: Find a place and say where you are going
lessons.introduction: The place is a slot. Its preposition and article are handled by the language, not by you inventing a new sentence.

notes.recipe: Wo ist + place? / Ich gehe + destination.
notes.explanation: Wo ist asks where something is. The destination expression after gehen changes depending on the place.
notes.detail: Memorize the chunks zum Bahnhof, zum Hotel, zur Toilette, and nach Hause. Prepositions and articles are combined in these forms.
notes.caution: Do not say “zu Hause” for motion. Nach Hause means going home; zu Hause means being at home.

lessons.title: Buying and paying
lessons.goal: Ask a price and pay for something
lessons.introduction: Combine price questions, purchasing and payment methods. Only the useful noun or payment method changes.

notes.recipe: Wie viel kostet + noun? / Kann ich mit Karte bezahlen?
notes.explanation: Use Wie viel kostet …? to ask a price. For permission to pay, Kann ich … bezahlen? follows the same modal pattern as the help requests.
notes.detail: Mit Karte means by card; bar means in cash. You can substitute a different noun phrase after kostet.
notes.caution: Kaffee is masculine, so the examples use einen Kaffee as the object but ein Kaffee as the subject of kostet.

examples.english: How much does a ticket cost?
How much does a coffee cost?
I want to buy a ticket.
I want to buy a coffee.

lessons.title: Today and tomorrow
lessons.goal: Situate a simple statement in time
lessons.introduction: Adding a time expression makes ordinary statements useful for near-future plans, without learning new tenses first.

notes.explanation: Heute means today; morgen means tomorrow. The finite verb remains second in statements, even when you add a time expression.
notes.detail: Present-tense German can express a scheduled near-future action when tomorrow makes the timing clear.
notes.caution: Morgen can also mean morning as a noun. Here it is the lowercase adverb “tomorrow.”

examples.english: I go to the hotel tomorrow.
I go to the station tomorrow.
I want to buy a ticket today.
examples.target: Ich will heute ein Ticket kaufen.

lessons.title: Say no and set limits
lessons.goal: Turn a positive sentence into a negative one
lessons.introduction: Negation is an operator: it changes the meaning of a clause, while each language decides where its negative words go.

notes.explanation: German distinguishes negating an action from saying you have or need none of something. Nicht typically negates actions; kein often negates indefinite noun phrases.
notes.detail: Compare Ich verstehe das nicht with Ich habe kein Ticket. In a modal construction, nicht commonly appears before the destination or final infinitive.
notes.caution: Kein changes like an article: kein Ticket, keine Zeit, keinen Kaffee. Learn each useful chunk rather than a full chart first.

examples.english: I do not have a ticket.
I cannot go to the station today.
examples.target: Ich kann heute nicht zum Bahnhof gehen.

lessons.title: Put the blocks together
lessons.introduction: Put a greeting, a question, a need and a request into separate short sentences. Complexity is optional.

notes.recipe: Entschuldigung. → Wo ist …? → Ich brauche … → Danke.
notes.explanation: Short sentences are enough. Start politely, ask one thing at a time, and check important details.
notes.detail: You can reuse the same few patterns across a station, hotel, supermarket, or café. These examples share predictable grammar.
notes.caution: Understanding a short answer from a native speaker may require more vocabulary than producing the question.

examples.english: How much does a ticket cost?
